Chronicle photo by Frederic Larson (RAW FILE)"},"articleBody":"The Golden Gate Bridge is the No. 1 suicide landmark in the world. Since it opened in 1937, an estimated 1,300 people have ended their lives by jumping off this monumental structure. My friend Mark Finch, former director of the San Francisco International Lesbian & Gay Film Festival, was one of them. Mark jumped Jan. 14, 1995. It was a rainy Saturday afternoon and no one saw him go over. His briefcase was found leaning against the railing at mid- span. His body drifted in the tides of the Pacific for nearly six weeks before being found, seven miles out to sea, off the coast from Pillar Point Harbor, some 25 miles south of where he had jumped. Combined statistics from the Marin County Coroner's Office and the San Francisco medical examiner indicate that there were 25 bodies identified as Golden Gate Bridge suicides in the year 2003, approximately one every two weeks. This official figure, however, does not take into account the bodies that are not recovered -- a figure that could be substantial due to the riptides and swift currents under the bridge. Local suicide-prevention experts believe the true suicide toll from the bridge is likely twice as high as the official reports indicate. In the decade since Mark's death, I have alternately avoided the bridge and felt compelled to discover more about it. What I've learned is simple, true and deeply melodramatic. If there had been a suicide barrier on the bridge, Mark would probably still be alive today. As early as February 1939 (after the bridge's 11th jumper), a San Francisco Call newspaper article noted that the California Highway Patrol was pondering the problem of how to prevent \"further suicidal leaps from the Bridge.\" A CHP officer presciently declared: \"Hardly 2 years old, the span gives promise of becoming a Mecca for despondent persons seeking self- destruction.\" The phenomenon of suicide landmarks is well documented. Examples include such lethal structures as the Eiffel Tower, Pasadena's Arroyo Seco Bridge, Japan's Mount Mihara and the Bloor Street Viaduct in Toronto. At all of these locations, suicides were halted by the erection of physical barriers. According to its official Web site (www.goldengate.org), the primary stated mission of the Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District is to: \"provide safe and reliable operation, maintenance and enhancement of the Golden Gate Bridge.\" Despite the prominent reference to safety in the district's mission statement, the board of directors has repeatedly decided against erecting a suicide barrier, most recently in 1999. Over the years, all of the arguments against a barrier have been dismantled: -- Engineering and wind shear concerns? In 1953, consulting engineer Clifford Paine told the bridge board that the railing could be raised an additional three feet with no negative impact on the bridge's structural integrity. -- Potential legal liability? In 1998, the Public Law Research Institute at Hastings College of Law issued a report, \"Civil Liability for Suicide Barriers,\" that determined that where public property has been the site of suicides in the past, building a barrier would not expose the entity administering the property to significant liability. -- Lack of funding? In 2003 construction was completed on a $5 million barrier between the pedestrian walkway and the bridge's traffic lanes, despite the fact that there has never been a pedestrian or cyclist fatality there; surely the bridge district can find funds for a project that would actually save lives. -- The notion that people prevented from jumping would only find a different way to kill themselves? In 1978, UC Berkeley psychologist who studies suicides, Richard Seiden, released the results of a study of more than 500 people who had been prevented from jumping off the Golden Gate Bridge between 1937 and 1971. The study showed that only about 6 percent had gone on to commit suicide in some other way. -- A barrier will ruin the view? The bridge district should follow the example of Toronto, which held a design competition in an effort to arrive at a satisfactory barrier for the Bloor Street Viaduct (formerly the No. 2 suicide magnet in North America). Architect Derick Revington's award-winning design (the $6 million \"luminous veil\" barrier) has been described as \"lifesaving art.\" It was completed in 2003 and has entirely halted suicides at that location. In the next few months, the Psychiatric Foundation of Northern California will launch a major campaign urging the bridge district to erect a barrier. A public-education campaign will be a significant part of this effort. (For more information or to support its efforts, visit the foundation's Web site at Chronicle photo by Frederic Larson (RAW FILE)</div></span><span class="photoCredit c-gray600 block rel z1 mt2 mr48"><span>FREDERIC LARSON</span></span></figcaption></figure><div class="pb20"><div id="everlit-auto-audio-widget" data-eid="item-103121" data-publication-id="pblc_qJWx3kIaE8Q" style="height:130px" class="x100 tac fs16"></div></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>The <a href="https://www.sfgate.com/golden-gate-bridge/" data-link="native" class="">Golden Gate Bridge</a> is the No. 1 suicide landmark in the world. Since it opened in 1937, an estimated 1,300 people have ended their lives by jumping off this monumental structure. My friend Mark Finch, former director of the San Francisco International Lesbian & Gay Film Festival, was one of them.</p></div><div data-eid="item-100634" id="" class="mb32 ar16-9 isolate z0 rel"><img src="https://cdn-channels-pixel.ex.co/events/0012000001fxZm9AAE?integrationType=DEFAULT&template=design%2Farticle%2Fplatypus_two_column.tpl" alt="" class="x1px y1px vh abs" aria-hidden="true" width="1" height="1"/><div id="30b0aaf4-cc13-4972-9cf9-ad9a05e5e62d" multiple=""></div></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>Mark jumped Jan. 14, 1995. It was a rainy Saturday afternoon and no one saw him go over. His briefcase was found leaning against the railing at mid- span. His body drifted in the tides of the Pacific for nearly six weeks before being found, seven miles out to sea, off the coast from Pillar Point Harbor, some 25 miles south of where he had jumped.</p></div><div class="pt16 sy16 bb bt b-gray300 mb32"><div class=""><p class="uiHeader11 f aic jcc ttu">Advertisement</p><p class="uiTextSmall f aic jcc">Article continues below this ad</p></div><div data-block-type="ad" data-small-id="A300" data-large-id="Inline-1" data-unit="hnp-sfgate.com/article_dtc" class="f jcc mnh250px sm:mnh600px ais lg:f lg:jcc lg:mnh250px lg:pb16 lg:aic"></div></div><div></div><div></div><div></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>Combined statistics from the Marin County Coroner's Office and the San Francisco medical examiner indicate that there were 25 bodies identified as Golden Gate Bridge suicides in the year 2003, approximately one every two weeks. This official figure, however, does not take into account the bodies that are not recovered -- a figure that could be substantial due to the riptides and swift currents under the bridge. Local suicide-prevention experts believe the true suicide toll from the bridge is likely twice as high as the official reports indicate.</p></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>In the decade since Mark's death, I have alternately avoided the bridge and felt compelled to discover more about it. What I've learned is simple, true and deeply melodramatic. If there had been a suicide barrier on the bridge, Mark would probably still be alive today.</p></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>As early as February 1939 (after the bridge's 11th jumper), a San Francisco Call newspaper article noted that the California Highway Patrol was pondering the problem of how to prevent "further suicidal leaps from the Bridge." A CHP officer presciently declared: "Hardly 2 years old, the span gives promise of becoming a Mecca for despondent persons seeking self- destruction."</p></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>The phenomenon of suicide landmarks is well documented. Examples include such lethal structures as the Eiffel Tower, Pasadena's Arroyo Seco Bridge, Japan's Mount Mihara and the Bloor Street Viaduct in Toronto. At all of these locations, suicides were halted by the erection of physical barriers.</p></div><div class="md:pt16 md:sy16 md:bb md:bt b-gray300 mb32"><div class="vh y0 mb0 md:vv md:y100 md:mb16"><p class="uiHeader11 f aic jcc ttu">Advertisement</p><p class="uiTextSmall f aic jcc">Article continues below this ad</p></div><div data-block-type="ad" data-small-id="NTV7ARD" data-large-id="Inline-2" data-unit="hnp-sfgate.com/article_dtc" class="lg:f lg:jcc lg:mnh250px lg:pb16 lg:aic"></div></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>According to its official Web site (<a href="http://www.goldengate.org" data-link="native" class="">www.goldengate.org</a>), the primary stated mission of the Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District is to: "provide safe and reliable operation, maintenance and enhancement of the Golden Gate Bridge." Despite the prominent reference to safety in the district's mission statement, the board of directors has repeatedly decided against erecting a suicide barrier, most recently in 1999.</p></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>Over the years, all of the arguments against a barrier have been dismantled:</p></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>-- Engineering and wind shear concerns? In 1953, consulting engineer Clifford Paine told the bridge board that the railing could be raised an additional three feet with no negative impact on the bridge's structural integrity.</p></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>-- Potential legal liability? In 1998, the Public Law Research Institute at Hastings College of Law issued a report, "Civil Liability for Suicide Barriers," that determined that where public property has been the site of suicides in the past, building a barrier would not expose the entity administering the property to significant liability.</p></div><div class="pt16 sy16 bb bt b-gray300 mb32"><div class=""><p class="uiHeader11 f aic jcc ttu">Advertisement</p><p class="uiTextSmall f aic jcc">Article continues below this ad</p></div><div data-block-type="ad" data-small-id="Inline-1" data-large-id="Inline-3" data-unit="hnp-sfgate.com/article_dtc" class="f jcc mnh250px pb16 aic lg:f lg:jcc lg:mnh250px lg:pb16 lg:aic"></div></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>-- Lack of funding? In 2003 construction was completed on a $5 million barrier between the pedestrian walkway and the bridge's traffic lanes, despite the fact that there has never been a pedestrian or cyclist fatality there; surely the bridge district can find funds for a project that would actually save lives.</p></div><div class="sy32 mb32"><div><div></div></div><div data-no-gen-eid="item-104954" class="none"></div><div data-no-gen-eid="item-105200" class="none"></div></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>-- The notion that people prevented from jumping would only find a different way to kill themselves? In 1978, UC Berkeley psychologist who studies suicides, Richard Seiden, released the results of a study of more than 500 people who had been prevented from jumping off the Golden Gate Bridge between 1937 and 1971. The study showed that only about 6 percent had gone on to commit suicide in some other way.</p></div><div class="r1udwkp5 d1uy5mhj articleBody mb32" data-block-type="text" data-dropcap="false"><p>-- A barrier will ruin the view? The bridge district should follow the example of Toronto, which held a design competition in an effort to arrive at a satisfactory barrier for the Bloor Street Viaduct (formerly the No. 2 suicide magnet in North America). Architect Derick Revington's award-winning design (the $6 million "luminous veil" barrier) has been described as "lifesaving art." Chronicle photo by Frederic Larson (RAW FILE)"},"articleBody":"The Golden Gate Bridge is the No. 1 suicide landmark in the world. Since it opened in 1937, an estimated 1,300 people have ended their lives by jumping off this monumental structure. My friend Mark Finch, former director of the San Francisco International Lesbian \u0026 Gay Film Festival, was one of them. Mark jumped Jan. 14, 1995. It was a rainy Saturday afternoon and no one saw him go over. His briefcase was found leaning against the railing at mid- span. His body drifted in the tides of the Pacific for nearly six weeks before being found, seven miles out to sea, off the coast from Pillar Point Harbor, some 25 miles south of where he had jumped. Combined statistics from the Marin County Coroner's Office and the San Francisco medical examiner indicate that there were 25 bodies identified as Golden Gate Bridge suicides in the year 2003, approximately one every two weeks. This official figure, however, does not take into account the bodies that are not recovered -- a figure that could be substantial due to the riptides and swift currents under the bridge. Local suicide-prevention experts believe the true suicide toll from the bridge is likely twice as high as the official reports indicate. In the decade since Mark's death, I have alternately avoided the bridge and felt compelled to discover more about it. What I've learned is simple, true and deeply melodramatic. If there had been a suicide barrier on the bridge, Mark would probably still be alive today. As early as February 1939 (after the bridge's 11th jumper), a San Francisco Call newspaper article noted that the California Highway Patrol was pondering the problem of how to prevent \"further suicidal leaps from the Bridge.\" A CHP officer presciently declared: \"Hardly 2 years old, the span gives promise of becoming a Mecca for despondent persons seeking self- destruction.\" The phenomenon of suicide landmarks is well documented. Examples include such lethal structures as the Eiffel Tower, Pasadena's Arroyo Seco Bridge, Japan's Mount Mihara and the Bloor Street Viaduct in Toronto. At all of these locations, suicides were halted by the erection of physical barriers. According to its official Web site (www.goldengate.org), the primary stated mission of the Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District is to: \"provide safe and reliable operation, maintenance and enhancement of the Golden Gate Bridge.\" Despite the prominent reference to safety in the district's mission statement, the board of directors has repeatedly decided against erecting a suicide barrier, most recently in 1999. Over the years, all of the arguments against a barrier have been dismantled: -- Engineering and wind shear concerns? In 1953, consulting engineer Clifford Paine told the bridge board that the railing could be raised an additional three feet with no negative impact on the bridge's structural integrity. -- Potential legal liability? In 1998, the Public Law Research Institute at Hastings College of Law issued a report, \"Civil Liability for Suicide Barriers,\" that determined that where public property has been the site of suicides in the past, building a barrier would not expose the entity administering the property to significant liability. -- Lack of funding? In 2003 construction was completed on a $5 million barrier between the pedestrian walkway and the bridge's traffic lanes, despite the fact that there has never been a pedestrian or cyclist fatality there; surely the bridge district can find funds for a project that would actually save lives. -- The notion that people prevented from jumping would only find a different way to kill themselves? In 1978, UC Berkeley psychologist who studies suicides, Richard Seiden, released the results of a study of more than 500 people who had been prevented from jumping off the Golden Gate Bridge between 1937 and 1971. The study showed that only about 6 percent had gone on to commit suicide in some other way. -- A barrier will ruin the view? The bridge district should follow the example of Toronto, which held a design competition in an effort to arrive at a satisfactory barrier for the Bloor Street Viaduct (formerly the No. 2 suicide magnet in North America). Architect Derick Revington's award-winning design (the $6 million \"luminous veil\" barrier) has been described as \"lifesaving art.\" It was completed in 2003 and has entirely halted suicides at that location. In the next few months, the Psychiatric Foundation of Northern California will launch a major campaign urging the bridge district to erect a barrier. A public-education campaign will be a significant part of this effort.
